_doc: GENERATED by scripts/native/gen-mediate.mjs from content/mediation/*.json (order = level then id, as web/cpack/mediation/index.js). source.kind: announcement|text|email|notice|talk (text = string|string[]) · dialogue (lines[{s,t}]) · chart (caption, cols, rows[[label,…]], unit, note). task.mode write|speak. points/leave_out checks = groups of phrases: a point is met when EVERY group has at least one phrase in the text (case-insensitive). Listen-first (text hidden until heard or Show text) for B2/C1/C2 except charts.

items.title: The pool is closed on Wednesdays
items.scenario: Your friend Lena takes her six-year-old son swimming every Wednesday afternoon. Her English is basic. She sends you a photo of a notice at the pool and asks what it says. Explain it in simple words.

text: SWIMMING POOL: NEW OPENING TIMES
From Monday 3 March the pool will close for cleaning every Wednesday from 12:00 to 16:00.
On Saturdays the pool now opens one hour earlier, at 8:00.
Children under 8 must always be with an adult.
Lockers need a coin. Please bring your own.
The cafe is closed until further notice.

task.audience: a friend who is learning English
task.prompt: Write a short message to Lena (30–55 words). Use easy words and short sentences. Tell her only what matters for her Wednesday visits.

points.idea: The pool is closed on Wednesdays.
It is closed from 12 to 4 in the afternoon.
This starts from 3 March.
Her young son must be with an adult.

items.model: Hi Lena! From 3 March the pool is closed every Wednesday from 12 to 4 in the afternoon, so please don't go then. Your son is only six, so he must always be with an adult. Maybe try another day this week!
useful: He must be with an adult.
tips: A sign talks to everybody. Your friend needs only the lines that change HER plan, so ignore the rest.
Say the day and the hours together (Wednesday, 12 to 4) so she can check them against her own plans.
items.explain: A good answer gives the day, the hours and the start date, and links the adult rule to her son. The Saturday time, the lockers and the cafe do not change her Wednesday plan.

items.title: A film afternoon for families
items.scenario: You hear this announcement at the community centre. Your neighbour Mr Ortiz has two grandchildren, aged four and nine, and loves to take them out. You meet him in the lift and tell him about it.

text: Good morning, everyone. This is Riverside Community Centre with news of this month's family film afternoon.
The film starts at three o'clock on Saturday 14 June in Hall B.
Tickets cost five dollars for adults. Children under five come in free.
You can buy popcorn at the door.
We are also looking for two volunteers to help with the chairs. Please speak to Mrs Lopez at the front desk.

task.audience: a neighbour with young grandchildren
task.prompt: Tell Mr Ortiz about the event (30–55 words). Say when and where it is and what it costs for his family.

points.idea: It is on Saturday 14 June at 3 o'clock.
It is in Hall B at the community centre.
Adults pay five dollars.
The four-year-old goes in free (under five).

items.model: Hello, Mr Ortiz! There's a film for families at the community centre. It's on Saturday 14 June at 3 in the afternoon, in Hall B. Adults pay five dollars, but your younger grandchild can come in free because she is under five.
useful: There's a film for families on …
It costs …, but children under … are free.
tips: Choose the details a person can act on: day, time, place, price. Then add the one fact that matters for THIS family (the free ticket).
When you speak, say the date and time slowly and in a clear order. The listener cannot go back and read it again.
items.explain: The listener needs when, where and the price, plus the free place for the under-five child. Popcorn and the call for volunteers are interesting but do not help Mr Ortiz decide or go.

items.title: How to take the cough syrup
items.scenario: Your flatmate Tom has a bad cough and a new bottle of syrup. He does not read English well and does not drive. He asks you to read the leaflet and tell him how to use it.

text: Honey-Lemon Cough Syrup. For adults and children over 6.
Take one spoon (5 ml) three times a day: in the morning, at lunchtime and before bed.
Do not take more than three spoons in one day.
Shake the bottle before use.
Do not drive if you feel sleepy.
Keep the bottle in a cool place. The syrup contains sugar.
Stop and see a doctor if your cough lasts more than seven days.

task.audience: a flatmate who cannot read the leaflet
task.prompt: Write a message to Tom (35–60 words) with the instructions he needs to take the syrup safely.

points.idea: One spoon each time.
Three times a day (morning, lunchtime, bed).
Never more than three spoons in a day.
See a doctor if the cough lasts more than seven days.

items.model: Hi Tom, the leaflet says you take one spoon of the syrup three times a day, morning, lunchtime and bedtime. Never take more than three spoons in a day. If your cough is still there after seven days, please go and see a doctor. Get well soon!
useful: Please go and see a doctor if …
tips: With medicine, numbers are the most important part: how much, how often, the daily maximum. Check each one twice.
Add a clear warning sign ("Never …", "see a doctor if …") so the reader knows what to do if something goes wrong.
items.explain: Tom must know the dose, the three times, the daily limit and when to see a doctor. Because he does not drive, the sleepiness warning can go; shaking, sugar and storage are small extras.

items.title: A customer with a noisy bike
items.scenario: You work in a bike shop. You took a phone call from a customer. Your colleague Dan repairs the bikes and is not in the shop today. Leave him a short note.

lines.t: Hello, I bought a red bike from you last month.
Yes, how can I help?
The front brake is very loud, and the bell does not work.
I am sorry to hear that. Would you like to bring it in?
Yes. I can come on Thursday after work, at about six. Please call my mobile, 555 0142, not my home number.
Fine. My colleague Dan will look at it.
Thank you. By the way, your shop window looks lovely this week!

task.audience: a colleague who repairs bikes
task.prompt: Write a note to Dan (30–50 words). Say what the customer wants and the details he needs.

points.idea: The brake is noisy and the bell is broken.
The customer brings it on Thursday at about six.
Call her mobile number.

leave_out.idea: The compliment about the shop window.

items.model: Dan, a customer is bringing her bike in on Thursday at about 6 in the evening. The front brake makes a very loud noise and the bell is broken. Please call her mobile on 555 0142 if you have any questions.
tips: A note for a colleague is a list of facts in sentences: what, when, how to contact. Skip the polite chat from the call.
Copy numbers and times exactly as you heard them. A wrong digit makes the whole note useless.
items.explain: Dan needs the two problems, the day and time, and the number. He does not need the bike colour or the compliment about the window.

items.title: The platform has changed
items.scenario: You are at a train station with your friend Sam, who doesn't speak much English. Sam was in the shop when an announcement came on. Sam texts you to ask what it said. Write a short message so Sam knows exactly what to do.

text: Good afternoon. This is an announcement for passengers travelling on the 14:35 service to Brighton.
Due to a signal problem near Croydon, this train will now depart from platform 9, not platform 4.
The train is also running about fifteen minutes late, and is now expected to leave at 14:50.
Please note that the front four coaches will be closed today, so passengers should board at the rear of the train.
Refreshments are available in the main concourse. We apologise for any inconvenience this may cause.

task.audience: a friend who missed the announcement
task.prompt: Write a text message to Sam (40–70 words). Tell Sam the three things that have changed and what to do. Leave out information Sam doesn't need.

points.idea: The train now leaves from platform 9 (not 4).
It is about 15 minutes late – it leaves at 14:50.
The front coaches are closed, so get on at the back.
A clear next step for Sam (meet / go now).

leave_out.idea: The reason (a signal problem near Croydon).

items.model: Hi Sam! Our train has moved to platform 9, not 4. It's also running about 15 minutes late, so it now leaves at 14:50. The front coaches are closed today, so we need to get on at the back of the train. Meet me by the stairs to platform 9 in five minutes, OK?
useful: We need to get on at the back.
Meet me by … in five minutes.
tips: Relaying means passing on what matters to THIS person: Sam needs where, when and what to do – not why the train is late.
Use your own simple words. Announcements are formal ("passengers should board at the rear"); a text to a friend is not ("get on at the back").
Finish with an action, so your friend knows the next step.
items.explain: A good relay keeps the three changes (platform 9, 14:50, board at the back), adds a clear next step, and drops the details that don't change what Sam does: the signal problem, the shop and the apology.

items.title: Remembering new words
items.scenario: You attended a short talk by your teacher, Mr Evans, about learning vocabulary. Your classmate Mia was ill and missed it. Send her your notes so she can follow the next class.

text: Today I would like to talk about how to remember new vocabulary. Many students read a word list ten times the night before a test. It feels useful, but research suggests it works badly.
A better method is spaced practice. Look at new words again after one day, then after three days, then after a week. Each review can be short, about ten minutes.
Second, do not only read. Cover the meaning and try to recall it. This effort feels hard, but it is exactly what builds memory.
Third, use the words in your own sentences. A word you have used is much harder to forget.
A quick note: the library has changed its opening hours this month, so check the board by the door.
Your homework is to choose twenty words from unit 4 and make a card for each one. Bring them next Tuesday, and we will test each other in pairs.

task.audience: a classmate who missed the talk
task.prompt: Write your notes for Mia (70–115 words). Include the main advice and what she has to do for the next class.

points.idea: Review words after a day, three days and a week.
Cover the meaning and try to remember it.
Use each word in your own sentence.
Homework: twenty words from unit 4 on cards, for Tuesday.

leave_out.idea: The bad habit of reading a list the night before.

items.model: Hi Mia, here are my notes from Mr Evans's talk. He said reading a word list again and again does not work well. Instead, look at new words after one day, three days and a week, for about ten minutes each time. Cover up the meaning and try to recall it, because that effort builds memory. Also write your own sentences with each word. For homework, make a card for each of twenty words from unit 4. Bring them on Tuesday, because we will test each other in pairs. See you in class!
tips: Notes for an absent person have two parts: the ideas they missed, and the jobs they must do. Do not forget the second part.
Name the speaker once ("Mr Evans said …") so Mia knows these are his points, then use short, direct sentences.
items.explain: Mia needs the three techniques (spaced review, recalling, own sentences) and the homework with its deadline. The library hours are a side comment and the night-before habit is only the speaker's warning.

items.title: Moving to the third floor
items.scenario: Your colleague Ravi has been on leave and comes back on Monday morning. His manager asks you to give him the essentials of this email, which has been sitting in his inbox.

text: Subject: Moving to the third floor
Dear all,

Our team moves to the third floor on Friday 20 September. To make the day easy, please put everything from your desk into the blue boxes by 5 pm on Thursday 19 September, and write your name on each box.
IT will move all computers, so please do not unplug your own.
If you use a standing desk, tell Facilities by noon on Monday 16 September so that one is ready for you upstairs.
The car park beside the building will be closed that Friday, but the new floor has a bigger kitchen with a coffee machine.
Thank you for your help.
Marta, Facilities

task.audience: a colleague returning from leave
task.prompt: Write a short message to Ravi (45–75 words). Say what is happening and what he must do. He uses a standing desk.

points.idea: The team moves to the third floor on Friday 20 September.
Pack his desk into the blue boxes by 5 pm on Thursday.
Write his name on each box.
Tell Facilities about his standing desk by noon today (Monday).

leave_out.idea: The new kitchen and coffee machine.

items.model: Hi Ravi, welcome back! Our move to the third floor is on Friday 20 September. Before then, please pack your desk by 5 pm on Thursday, using the blue boxes, and put your name on each one. Since you use a standing desk, you also need to tell Facilities by noon today, Monday, or there won't be one ready for you.
useful: Since you …, you also need to …
tips: Start from the action. In a work email, the first question is "what do I have to do, and by when?" Put deadlines next to the actions.
Use what you know about the reader. Only Ravi has a standing desk, so that line must be in his message, and the weekend details are not.
items.explain: The summary needs the move date, the packing deadline and labels, and Ravi's own deadline for the standing desk. The car park and the new coffee machine are background.

items.title: What students eat at lunch
items.scenario: You help in the school office. The cook, Ms Okoye, is on the phone and cannot see the lunch survey. She has to decide whether to prepare more hot meals next term. Explain what the chart shows.

source.caption: What students chose for lunch (% of students)

task.audience: the school cook, who cannot see the chart
task.prompt: Explain the chart to Ms Okoye in about 40 seconds (45–70 words). Say what changed most and what it could mean for her decision.

points.idea: Hot meals rose from 35% to 48% and are now the most popular.
Sandwiches fell from 40% to 31%.
Fewer students bring food from home.
She could prepare more hot meals.

items.model: Hello, Ms Okoye. The chart shows what students ate at lunch in September and in March. Hot meals are now the most popular choice: they went up from 35% to 48%. Sandwiches have fallen, from 40% to 31%, and fewer students bring packed lunches from home. So I think you should prepare more hot meals next term.
tips: For a listener who cannot see the chart, say what the chart is about first, then give only the biggest changes with the "from … to …" figures.
Finish with what the numbers mean for the person's decision. Facts without a conclusion leave the work to the listener.
items.explain: Ms Okoye needs the two big movements (hot meals up, sandwiches down), the drop in packed lunches, and a simple recommendation. The small salad change does not affect her decision.

items.title: Who was going to clean the kitchen?
items.scenario: You share a flat with Ana and Ben. They are annoyed with each other about the kitchen, and you overhear this. You decide to help them understand each other.

lines.t: You said you would clean the kitchen. It is still a mess!
I said I would do it after the weekend. I meant Monday.
I thought you meant Saturday. My parents came on Sunday and the kitchen was awful.
I did not know your parents were coming. You never told me.
I wrote it in the group chat on Wednesday.
I muted that chat. It is full of memes.

task.audience: two flatmates who are upset with each other
task.prompt: Speak to Ana and Ben (55–90 words). Explain what each of them meant, in a friendly way, and suggest how to avoid the problem again.

points.idea: Ben meant he would clean on Monday, after the weekend.
Ana thought he meant Saturday because her parents were visiting.
Ben did not see the message because he muted the chat.
Agree a day and write it down.

items.model: Let me check that I've understood you both. Ben, you meant you would clean the kitchen on Monday, after the weekend. Ana, you thought he meant Saturday, because your parents were coming on Sunday. And Ben didn't know about the visit, because he had muted the group chat. So nobody was wrong, really. It was a misunderstanding. Why don't we agree on one day now and write it on the fridge?
useful: Let me check that I've understood you both.
tips: To calm a small conflict, say what each person meant before you say anything else. People relax when they hear their own point described fairly.
Use "you meant … / you thought …" for both sides in the same shape, so neither person feels you chose a favourite.
items.explain: The speaker explains Ben's plan (Monday), Ana's understanding (Saturday, parents), the muted chat, and a fix. Repeating the blame and the jokes about memes would not help the two of them.

items.title: How plants make food
items.scenario: Your classmate Jun finds this sentence in a science textbook too difficult and asks you to explain it in plain English.

text: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis, a process in which light energy, absorbed by chlorophyll in the leaves, is used to convert water and carbon dioxide into glucose and oxygen.
The glucose provides the plant with the energy it needs to grow, whereas the oxygen is released into the air as a by-product.
Without sufficient light, the rate of this process falls, which is why plants kept in dark rooms often grow weak and pale.

task.audience: a classmate who finds the textbook too hard
task.prompt: Explain the paragraph to Jun in simple words (60–95 words). Do not copy the textbook words.

points.idea: Plants use light to make their own food.
They take in water and carbon dioxide.
They produce sugar (glucose) and oxygen.
Without enough light, plants become weak.

items.model: Jun, this is simpler than it looks. Plants make their own food using light from the sun. The leaves take in water and carbon dioxide, and the light turns them into sugar and oxygen. The plant uses the sugar to grow, and it lets the oxygen go into the air. If a plant gets too little light, it cannot make enough food, so it becomes weak and pale. That is why plants in dark rooms look sick.
useful: It is simpler than it looks.
tips: To simplify a hard sentence, find the main verb and the main idea first. Then rebuild it in two or three short sentences.
Replace technical terms with everyday words. Keep only the ones the reader will need later in the exam.
items.explain: A good answer keeps the whole process (light, water and carbon dioxide in; sugar and oxygen out) and the effect of too little light. It drops chlorophyll and by-product, which make the text harder without changing the idea.

items.title: Planning the open day
items.scenario: You were in the team meeting below. Your colleague Sam could not come, and the meeting gave Sam a job. Send Sam an email with the main points.

lines.t: Right, three things today: the date, the budget and who does what.
Can we hold the open day on 12 October? The hall is free that Saturday.
Fine, let us confirm 12 October. We have 400 for food and posters.
I would rather spend 150 on posters and the rest on food.
OK. Omar, can you design the posters by next Friday?
Yes. And the coffee machine is broken again, but that is another story.
Sam could not come, so Sam has a job: please ask every team how many people will come, and send the number to Lena by the 30th.

task.audience: a colleague who missed the meeting
task.prompt: Write an email to Sam (50–80 words) with the decisions and Sam's own job.

points.idea: The open day is on Saturday 12 October.
Sam must ask the teams how many people will come.
Send the number to Lena by the 30th.
Omar will design the posters by next Friday.

items.model: Hi Sam, here is what we decided in the meeting. The open day will be on Saturday 12 October, and Omar is designing the posters by next Friday. Your job is to ask every team how many people are coming. Please send that number to Lena by the 30th, because she is ordering the food. Thanks, and let me know if anything is unclear.
useful: Let me know if anything is unclear.
tips: Meeting notes for an absent person should separate decisions ("what is fixed") from actions ("who does what by when").
Put the reader's own task in its own sentence, with a name and a deadline, so it cannot be missed.
items.explain: Sam needs the date, Omar's posters (as context) and, above all, Sam's own job with the person and deadline. The broken coffee machine is off-topic, and the exact budget split does not affect Sam.

items.title: How our town gets to work
items.scenario: You volunteer for a local transport group. Your colleague Priya is on the phone and can't see the survey chart. She has to decide whether to ask the council for more cycle lanes or more buses. Explain what the data shows so she can decide.

source.caption: How residents usually travel to work (% of people surveyed, 2016 and 2026)

task.audience: a colleague who can't see the chart and has to make a decision
task.prompt: Explain the chart to Priya in about one minute (90–140 words). Give the overall picture first, then the two biggest changes with figures, and say what it might mean for her decision. Don't read out every number.

points.idea: Overall: the car is still the most common way, but much less than before.
Car use fell sharply, from 58% to 41%.
Cycling more than tripled, from 6% to 19%.
Bus use stayed roughly the same (17% → 15%).
What it suggests for the decision (demand is growing for cycling, not buses), with a cautious word.

leave_out.idea: Reading out the walking figures one by one (14% → 13%) – they don't affect the decision.

items.model: OK, so the chart compares how people got to work in 2016 and 2026. Overall, the car is still the most common way, but it's dropped a lot – from 58% to 41%. The biggest change is cycling: it's more than tripled, from 6% to 19%, so almost one in five people now cycle. Buses, on the other hand, have hardly changed – around 15 to 17%. Walking is about the same too, and more people work from home now. So if you're choosing between the two, the data suggests that demand is growing for cycling rather than buses. More cycle lanes would probably match what people are already doing – though we might want to ask bus users why they aren't switching.
useful: Overall, … is still the most common …, but …
The biggest change is … : it's gone from … to …
tips: Someone who can't see a chart needs the big picture first, then two or three key numbers – not a list of every figure.
Round and compare: "almost one in five", "more than tripled" are easier to follow on the phone than "19 per cent" alone.
End with what the data means for the listener's decision, and hedge it (suggests, probably) – a survey doesn't prove everything.
items.explain: A strong answer gives the overview (cars still first but falling), the two biggest changes with figures (car 58→41, cycling 6→19), notes that buses barely changed, and links this cautiously to Priya's decision.

items.title: The case for a real lunch break
items.scenario: Your manager Elena is thinking about encouraging a lunchtime walk in her team. She has no time to read the article below. Summarise it for her, including what the writer thinks.

text: Few of us now leave the desk at lunchtime. A recent survey of 2,000 office workers in one region found that fewer than one in four take a proper break away from the screen, and nearly half admit to eating while answering messages. Many managers see this as dedication. I think it is a false economy.

Studies of attention are consistent: after about ninety minutes of concentrated work, performance falls, and a real break, ideally outdoors, restores it. In a trial at a small design studio, staff who walked for twenty minutes at midday made around a third fewer errors in the afternoon than colleagues who stayed at their desks.

Critics argue that a walk is a luxury when deadlines are tight. But the studio saw no drop in output: the walkers finished the same work in the same time, with fewer corrections. The real obstacle is cultural, because nobody wants to be the first to leave. Leaders therefore have to go first, and say openly that breaks are expected, not merely tolerated.
Of course, a lunch walk will not fix an unrealistic workload, and it is no substitute for fair deadlines. But as a cheap, quick change it deserves a fairer trial in more workplaces than it gets.

task.audience: a manager deciding whether to try a new habit
task.prompt: Write a summary for Elena (90–140 words). Keep the writer's main argument, the key evidence and the limits the writer admits.

points.idea: The writer thinks skipping breaks is a false economy.
In a studio trial, walkers made about a third fewer errors with the same output.
The obstacle is culture, so leaders must go first.
A walk will not fix an unrealistic workload.

items.model: Elena, the writer argues that working through lunch is a false economy. Staff rarely take real breaks, and managers often mistake this for commitment. The key evidence comes from a design studio: employees who took a twenty-minute walk at midday made about a third fewer errors in the afternoon, and still produced the same amount of work. According to the writer, the main obstacle is culture, since nobody wants to leave first, so leaders must set the example and make breaks normal. However, the writer admits that a walk will not solve an unrealistic workload. It is a cheap change that is worth a proper trial, and your team could be a good place to start.
tips: A summary keeps the author's position, not only the facts. Say what the writer thinks ("argues", "admits") so the reader knows what is opinion.
Keep one piece of evidence with its main figure and leave out the supporting statistics that the argument does not depend on.
items.explain: The summary needs the stance, the best evidence, the point about leaders and the writer's limit. The survey size and the ninety-minute figure are supporting detail that Elena does not need to decide.

items.title: Electric bike or ordinary bike?
items.scenario: Your friend Jonas has a 12 km commute with one steep hill. He lives on the third floor, with no lift, and is deciding which bike to buy. He has not read this article, so tell him what it says that applies to him.

text: Choosing a commuter bike usually comes down to two options, and each has real strengths.

An electric bike gives a push on hills and in headwinds, so riders arrive faster and far less sweaty. This matters most on rides over ten kilometres. It also makes carrying shopping easy. On the other hand, it typically costs four or five times as much as an ordinary bike, it is heavy, often over twenty kilograms, so carrying it upstairs is hard, and the battery needs charging after about forty kilometres. Thieves also target electric models.

An ordinary bike is cheaper, light enough to lift, and needs no charging. It is also simple to repair. However, hills are tiring, riders often arrive hot, and long trips can feel like a chore, which means some owners stop cycling in winter.

Neither choice is correct for everyone. Weigh your distance, your hills and, importantly, where you will store the bike. The first electric bikes appeared in the 1890s, but only recently have batteries become light enough for them to be popular.

task.audience: a friend who must decide what to buy
task.prompt: Write a message to Jonas (80–120 words). Explain the main pros and cons and say which points matter most for his situation.

points.idea: The electric bike helps with hills and he arrives less sweaty.
It costs much more than an ordinary bike.
It is heavy to carry up to a third-floor flat.
The battery lasts about 40 km, enough for his 24 km round trip.
A recommendation tied to Jonas.

items.model: Hi Jonas, I read that article for you. In short, an electric bike would help with your hill and you would arrive far less sweaty on a 12 km ride. The battery lasts about 40 km, so your 24 km round trip is fine. The downsides are the price, which is about four or five times higher, and the weight: it is heavy to carry up to your third-floor flat. In your case, I'd think hard about where you can keep it. If you can park it safely downstairs, I'd go electric; if not, an ordinary bike may be easier.
useful: If …, I'd go for …; if not, …
tips: When you relay pros and cons for a decision, sort them by relevance to the person, not by their order in the text.
Do some small calculations for the reader (12 km each way = 24 km a day). Linking the text to their life is what makes it useful.
items.explain: Jonas needs the hill and sweat benefit, the cost, the weight on the stairs, and the battery range checked against his commute, with a recommendation. The history of electric bikes does not help his choice.

items.title: Office days or home days?
items.scenario: You chair a short team meeting. Dana and Tomas disagree about the new working pattern and are talking past each other. Help them understand each other's views and move towards a decision.

lines.t: On home days I finish more in a morning than I do in a whole day here. Nobody walks up to my desk every ten minutes.
But that is exactly the point. Our new starters learn by overhearing and asking quick questions. If everybody works from home, they lose that.
Then let them book a call. We do not need to sit in a room just to be available. Anyway, Tomas just likes an audience.
That is unfair. I am worried about the juniors, not about myself. And a call is not the same as a quick question across the desk.
Fine. But the coffee in this office is terrible, and the commute costs me two hours a day.
I am not saying everyone must come in five days. I just want us to be in at the same time sometimes.

task.audience: two colleagues who disagree in a meeting
task.prompt: Speak to Dana and Tomas (80–130 words). Show that you understand each view, name what they share, and suggest a practical way forward.

points.idea: Dana needs quiet days to concentrate.
Tomas worries that new starters learn less without informal contact.
Both want the team to work well and do not want five office days.
Try shared office days as a trial.

leave_out.idea: The remark about Tomas liking an audience.

items.model: Thank you both. Let me check I've understood. Dana, you get your best work done on home days because nobody interrupts you, so you need that time to focus. Tomas, you're worried that new starters will learn less if nobody is around to ask quick questions. I think you both want the same thing: a team that works well, and neither of you is asking for five days in the office. So how about a trial? We could agree on two shared office days, keep the other days flexible, and look at how it works after a month. Would that be acceptable to you both?
useful: I think you both want the same thing: …
Would that be acceptable to you both?
tips: Before you propose anything, describe each person's underlying need (focus, learning), not their position (home vs office). Needs overlap more than positions.
Leave out remarks about people ("just likes an audience") and respond only to the reasons. This keeps the discussion on the problem.
items.explain: The facilitator names Dana's need, Tomas's worry, what they share, and a small reversible trial. Repeating the personal jibe or the coffee complaint would add heat without helping.

items.title: How a heat pump works
items.scenario: Your neighbour Mr Brandt is thinking about replacing his old gas boiler. He has no technical background and asks you what a heat pump is after you heard this talk at a home energy fair.

text: Good afternoon. People are often puzzled by the name, so let me start with what a heat pump does not do: it does not create heat by burning anything. Instead, it moves heat from one place to another.

Even cold outdoor air contains some heat. A fluid called a refrigerant circulates in a sealed loop. In the evaporator, it absorbs heat from the outside air and turns into a gas. A compressor then squeezes that gas, which makes it much hotter. In the condenser, the hot gas passes its heat to the water in your radiators and turns back into a liquid. The cycle then repeats.
It is the same principle as your fridge, only in reverse: a fridge moves heat out of the cold box and into the kitchen.

Because the pump moves heat instead of making it, it is very efficient. For every unit of electricity it uses, it typically delivers about three units of heat. It keeps working in freezing weather, although it uses more electricity then.
There are two caveats. The equipment costs more to install than a gas boiler, and it works best in a well-insulated home, where the heat stays inside.

task.audience: an older neighbour with no technical background
task.prompt: Explain to Mr Brandt how a heat pump works and whether it might suit him (75–120 words). Use everyday language and a comparison.

points.idea: It moves heat from outside to inside instead of burning fuel.
It works even when it is cold outside.
It gives about three units of heat for one of electricity.
It costs more to install and suits a well-insulated house.

items.model: Mr Brandt, a heat pump doesn't make heat by burning gas. It simply moves heat from the outside air into your house, a bit like a fridge working in reverse. Even cold air has some heat in it, so it keeps working in winter. And it is very efficient: for every one unit of electricity, you get about three units of warmth. There are two things to think about. It costs more to install than a boiler, and it is most effective in a well-insulated house, so it may be worth checking your windows and roof first.
useful: a bit like a … working in reverse
for every one …, you get about …
There are two things to think about.
tips: To explain a process to a non-specialist, begin with the key idea in one sentence, then use a familiar comparison (a fridge) instead of the parts.
End a simple explanation with how it applies to the listener, so the idea becomes a decision they can make.
items.explain: Mr Brandt needs the basic idea (moving heat), that it works in cold, the three-for-one efficiency, and the cost and insulation conditions. The names of the parts would only confuse him.

items.title: Where support requests come from
items.scenario: You read the quarterly support report. Your colleague Hugo plans the team's rota and wants to know what matters without reading it. Brief him in an email.

source.caption: Customer support requests by channel (number of tickets per quarter)
source.note: Average wait for a first reply in Q3: chat 9 minutes (target: 2 minutes), phone under 1 minute, email 6 hours.

task.audience: a colleague who plans the staff rota
task.prompt: Write an email to Hugo (70–115 words). Highlight what matters for staffing and suggest what to do. You need not list every figure.

points.idea: Chat nearly doubled, from 2,100 to 3,900.
Email is still the biggest channel but is falling.
Chat customers wait 9 minutes against a 2-minute target.
Move some staff to chat.

items.model: Hi Hugo, here is what matters in the support report for the rota. Chat has almost doubled, from 2,100 tickets in Q1 to 3,900 in Q3. Email is still the biggest channel with 4,100 tickets, but it is falling, and phone is down too. The problem is that chat customers now wait about 9 minutes for a first reply, while our target is 2 minutes. I would suggest moving some agents from email to chat next month. I can send you the full report if you want the details.
useful: Here is what matters in the report for …
tips: Briefing someone on a report starts with their job. Hugo schedules people, so volumes and waiting times matter more than totals.
Join a trend to a problem and then to an action (chat is growing, replies are slow, so move staff). That chain is what makes data useful.
items.explain: Hugo needs the growth in chat, the status of email, the waiting-time gap and a staffing suggestion. The small social media numbers do not change the rota.

items.title: What does it cost to cancel?
items.scenario: You work in the office of a craft centre. A customer, Ms Adams, has emailed to cancel her pottery workshop booking for 20 June. It is now 11 June. She asks what she will have to pay. Reply politely, using the fee chart.

source.caption: Cancellation fees for workshop bookings (% of the ticket price)
source.note: Fees apply to the ticket price. A booking can be transferred to another person free of charge at any time.

task.audience: a customer who wants to cancel
task.prompt: Write a reply to Ms Adams (70–110 words). Say what her fee would be, explain the alternative, and be polite and clear.

points.idea: Cancelling now (nine days before) costs 25%.
Waiting would raise the fee, to 50% from 2 to 6 days before.
She can pass the booking to someone else at no cost.
Ask her to tell you what she decides.

leave_out.idea: The 100% fee for very late cancellations.
The free-cancellation rule for 14 days or more.

items.model: Dear Ms Adams, thank you for your message. Your workshop is nine days away, so if you cancel today the fee would be 25% of the ticket price. Please note that this would rise to 50% if you cancel later this week, so it is better to decide soon. Another option is to transfer your booking to a friend or someone else, which is free at any time. Please let me know what you would like to do, and I will arrange it. Kind regards, the booking office.
useful: Your workshop is … days away, so …
Please let me know what you would like to do.
tips: Apply the table to this person's date before you write. Telling Ms Adams "25%" is clearer than reading out four lines of a chart.
In a customer reply, offer the cheaper choice (a free transfer) clearly, not buried at the end, and close with the next step.
items.explain: Ms Adams needs her own fee, the warning that it grows, the free transfer and a next step. The extreme end of the chart (100%, free cancellation) does not apply to her situation.

items.title: Closing the street on Sundays
items.scenario: You chair a residents' meeting. Rosa and Ivan disagree about closing the high street to traffic on Sundays. The talk is getting heated. Speak to them and the room to find common ground.

lines.t: My children cannot even cross the road safely on a Sunday. Closing the street would give them a safe place to play and ride their bikes.
And who pays for that? Sunday is my best day. If drivers cannot reach my shop, my customers will simply go elsewhere.
You only care about money. This is about children.
I care about a street that has shops left in ten years. I would love families to come. I just do not want them to be turned away at the corner.
Nobody would be turned away. People can walk.
Not everyone can walk, Rosa. My regular customers are elderly and many drive.

task.audience: two neighbours with opposing views, and the room
task.prompt: Speak as the chair (85–135 words). Do justice to both positions, point to what they share, and suggest a compromise to test.

points.idea: Rosa's concern is the safety of children on the road.
Ivan fears his customers, many elderly, cannot reach the shops.
Both want a lively, welcoming street for families.
Try a time-limited trial (e.g. three months, afternoons only).
Check whether both can accept it.

items.model: Thank you, Rosa and Ivan. I think we are hearing two sincere concerns. Rosa, you want children to be safe on the road and to have room to play. Ivan, you are worried that elderly customers who drive will not be able to reach your shop. In fact, you both want the same thing: a lively street where families feel welcome. So let me suggest a small trial. We could close the street for three months, but only on Sunday afternoons, keep a few parking spaces for older drivers at the end of the road, and then look at the results together. Would that be something you could both accept?
useful: I think we are hearing two sincere concerns.
So let me suggest a small trial.
Would that be something you could both accept?
tips: Name the value behind each position (safety, access) in words both speakers would accept, then say what they share before you suggest anything.
Propose a limited, time-boxed trial rather than a permanent change. People agree to experiments more easily than to rules.
items.explain: The chair states Rosa's and Ivan's concerns fairly, names the shared goal, proposes a time-limited trial and checks acceptance. Repeating "you only care about money" would not help find common ground.

items.title: Should short-term lets be capped?
items.scenario: Councillor Varga is preparing for a housing committee and has asked you for a precise summary of this opinion essay. She needs the argument with its distinctions, not a list of headlines.

text: When I rented a flat for a fortnight last summer, the owner proudly told me that it had changed her life. I mention it only because stories like hers dominate the debate over short-term holiday lets, and they tell us little about what a city should do.

Advocates of strict limits point to a clear pattern: neighbourhoods with many holiday lets have seen rents rise faster than elsewhere. The trouble is that this is a correlation. Popular districts attract both tourists and higher rents, so we cannot yet say which causes which. The best studies, which compare similar districts before and after new rules, suggest a real but modest effect, and one concentrated in a handful of central streets rather than across the whole city.

This matters because blanket bans are sold as a way of returning homes to long-term tenants. Evidence from cities that have tried them is discouraging: many of the properties were sold, left empty or converted to other commercial uses, and few reappeared on the rental market. A ban can therefore remove a nuisance without delivering the benefit that justified it.

None of this means that nothing should be done. A mandatory register of every listing would give the council data it currently lacks, and an annual cap on the number of nights a whole home can be let, set more tightly in the most affected streets, would target the problem where it exists. Such a system is harder to design than a ban, but it is likelier to achieve what voters actually want.
Where hosts rent a spare room in their own home, the harm is much smaller and the rules should be lighter still.

task.audience: a city councillor preparing for a committee
task.prompt: Write a summary for Councillor Varga (95–150 words). Keep the writer's distinctions (what is proven and what is not) and the policy conclusion.

points.idea: Rents rose faster where there are many lets, but this is a correlation, so causation is unproven.
The effect is modest and concentrated in a few central areas.
Bans often fail because the homes do not return to the long-term rental market.
The writer prefers a register and a cap on nights, tighter in affected streets.
Renting a spare room does little harm and should face lighter rules.

leave_out.idea: The opening anecdote about the writer's holiday.

items.model: Councillor, the writer argues against blanket bans on short-term lets and for a targeted system. The evidence is weaker than campaigners claim: rents did rise faster where lets are common, but this is only a correlation, as popular districts draw both tourists and higher rents. The better studies find a real but modest effect, concentrated in a few central streets. Bans are also disappointing in practice, because the homes concerned were mostly sold, left empty or put to other commercial uses instead of returning to long-term tenants. The writer therefore favours a compulsory register and an annual cap on nights, stricter in the worst-affected streets. Renting a spare room in one's own home does little harm and should be regulated more lightly.
useful: The writer argues against … and for …
The evidence is weaker than … claim
this is only a correlation, as …
tips: Accurate summaries of demanding texts keep the writer's qualifications. "A real but modest effect" is not the same claim as "a big effect".
Separate three layers for the reader: what the evidence shows, what it does not show, and what the writer recommends.
items.explain: The councillor needs the correlation-versus-cause distinction, the limited and local effect, why bans disappoint, the alternative policy and the lighter rule for spare rooms. The holiday anecdote is only a hook.

items.title: A letter about housing support
items.scenario: Your friend Mr Okafor arrived in the country recently and received this letter. He understands everyday English but not official language. Turn it into a list of actions he can follow.

text: Reference: HS/2291/08
Dear Mr Okafor,

We refer to your application for housing support received on 3 February, and apologise for the delay in responding. In accordance with Section 14 of the Housing Assistance Regulations, your application has been provisionally accepted, subject to the completion of the enclosed Form B and the supply of the supporting evidence described below.

You are required to return the completed Form B, either by post or through the online portal, no later than 15 March, quoting the reference number shown above. Applications that reach us after this date will be treated as withdrawn and a fresh application will be needed.

Form B must be accompanied by documentary proof of your household income for the preceding three months, which may take the form of payslips or bank statements. Please note that originals are not required; clear copies will suffice.

At this stage no payment is due. Should the application be approved, a separate notice will set out any contribution payable and the date from which support begins. Please do not make any payment in response to unsolicited messages claiming to come from this department.
Any change in your address, income or the number of people in your household must be notified in writing within 14 days of the change taking effect.
Yours sincerely, Housing Support Team

task.audience: a friend who is new to official English
task.prompt: Write a numbered list of what Mr Okafor must do (100–155 words in total). Use plain language and include any deadline.

points.idea: Return Form B by 15 March, by post or online, with the reference number.
Attach proof of income for the last three months (copies are fine).
If it is late, the application is cancelled and he must start again.
Do not pay anything now, and ignore messages asking for money.
Tell them in writing within 14 days of any change.

leave_out.idea: The legal reference (Section 14) and the apology for the delay.

items.model:
Mr Okafor, here is what the letter asks you to do.
1. Fill in the Form B that came with the letter. Send it back by 15 March, by post or on the website, and write the reference number HS/2291/08 on it.
2. Add proof of how much money your household earned in the last three months. Payslips or bank statements are fine, and copies are enough.
3. Do not be late. If the form arrives after 15 March, your application is cancelled and you will have to apply again.
4. Do not pay anything now, and ignore any message that asks you for money.
5. If your address, income or number of people at home changes, tell them in writing within 14 days.
useful: Here is what the letter asks you to do.
If it arrives after …, you will have to …
ignore any message that asks you for …
tips: Turn each formal obligation ("you are required to…") into a short command with a verb first. The list should be usable without the letter.
Keep identifiers the reader will need (the reference number, the date) and drop the legal framing that does not change what they do.
items.explain: The action list covers the form with its deadline and reference, proof of income, the consequence of lateness, the no-payment warning and the 14-day rule. The regulation number and the apology are courtesy and legal wording.

items.title: Terms of a broadband contract
items.scenario: Ms Duarte runs a small shop and is about to sign a broadband agreement. She asks you what the key conditions mean in practice. Explain them in plain language in an email.

text: 4. Term and termination. 4.1 The Initial Term of this Agreement shall be twenty-four (24) months from the Service Start Date. 4.2 Should the Customer terminate this Agreement before the expiry of the Initial Term for any reason other than the Provider's material breach, the Customer shall pay an early termination charge equal to fifty per cent (50%) of the monthly charges remaining until the expiry of the Initial Term. 4.3 Upon expiry of the Initial Term, this Agreement shall continue on a rolling monthly basis unless terminated by either party on not less than thirty (30) days' written notice.

5. Charges. 5.1 The Provider may increase the monthly charges once in any twelve-month period by an amount not exceeding the annual rate of inflation published by the national statistics office plus two per cent (2%). 5.2 Invoices are payable within fourteen days of the invoice date.

6. Equipment. 6.1 All equipment supplied remains the property of the Provider and must be returned within fourteen (14) days of termination, failing which a charge of sixty (60) currency units shall apply.

9. Liability and governing law. 9.1 The Provider's aggregate liability under this Agreement shall not exceed the charges paid in the preceding twelve months. 9.2 This Agreement is governed by the laws of the Provider's country of registration.

task.audience: a small-business owner who must sign the contract
task.prompt: Write an email to Ms Duarte (95–150 words) that explains what she is agreeing to, in plain English and without legal language.

points.idea: She is committed for 24 months.
Leaving early costs half of the remaining monthly fees.
The price can rise once a year, by inflation plus 2%.
After 24 months it continues monthly; ending it needs 30 days' written notice.
The equipment must be returned within 14 days or she pays 60.

leave_out.idea: The liability limit and the governing law.

items.model: Dear Ms Duarte, here is what the contract means in plain words. You are committing to the service for 24 months. If you leave before then, you will pay half of the monthly fees that are left, so please be sure about the length. The company can raise the price once a year, by the inflation rate plus 2%. When the 24 months end, the contract simply carries on month by month, and you can stop it by giving 30 days' notice in writing. Finally, the router and other equipment belong to the company: if you do not send them back within 14 days of leaving, you will be charged 60. Please call me if you would like to go through any point together.
tips: Replace each defined legal term with the real-life consequence ("Initial Term" becomes "you are tied in for 24 months").
For a client, flag the clause that can cost money (early exit, equipment) in words that show the risk, and leave out clauses that cannot change her decision.
items.explain: Ms Duarte needs the length, the exit cost, the price-rise formula, the notice rule and the equipment return. The liability cap and the governing-law clause matter to lawyers, not to her signing decision.

items.title: Database migration update
items.scenario: You took part in the engineering meeting below. The Chief Operating Officer and the directors need a short email: what happened, what it means and what they must decide.

lines.t: Status: the migration planned for 3 June cannot go ahead. The payment module failed two of the six acceptance tests last night.
Both failures are in refund handling. If we went live like this, some refunds would be processed twice.
Exactly. So we are proposing a new date of 24 June. That gives us three weeks to fix and retest.
Can the current team do it by then?
Not without help. We need a specialist contractor for about three weeks. The quote is 12,000.
We need a decision from management by Friday, otherwise even 24 June is at risk.
Before we close, shall we change the dashboard colours to match the new brand? Blue looks better to me.
That is for the design team. Let us stay on the migration.

task.audience: senior managers who were not at the meeting
task.prompt: Write a short email to the Chief Operating Officer and the directors (85–130 words). State the situation, the cause, the cost and what you need from them.

points.idea: The 3 June migration is postponed to 24 June.
The payment module failed acceptance tests (refunds could be processed twice).
A contractor costs 12,000 for about three weeks.
Management must approve by Friday or the new date is at risk.

leave_out.idea: The side discussion about dashboard colours.

items.model: Dear all, a short update on the database migration. We cannot go live on 3 June, because two of the six acceptance tests for the payment module failed. The faults are in refund handling and could cause some refunds to be processed twice, so launching now would be unsafe. We propose a new date of 24 June, which allows three weeks to fix and retest. The current team cannot meet that date alone: a specialist contractor is needed for roughly three weeks, at a cost of 12,000. Could you please approve this by Friday? Without a decision by then, even 24 June is at risk. Kind regards.
useful: We cannot go live on …, because …
We propose a new date of …
Could you please approve this by …?
tips: Senior readers want the decision first. Put the situation, the reason, the cost and the question in that order, in a few lines.
Give the consequence of delay ("even 24 June is at risk") so managers can see why the deadline for their answer is real.
items.explain: The email needs the new date, the cause and its risk, the contractor cost and the approval deadline. The tangent about dashboard colours was dismissed in the meeting and has no place in a management briefing.

items.title: Do sleep programmes work in schools?
items.scenario: Five small studies tested the same school sleep programme. Dr Mensah, the head teacher, cannot read the research summary in time. Explain where the studies agree and disagree, so she can judge whether to adopt it.

source.caption: Five studies of a school sleep programme for teenagers
source.note: Studies A and E took place in boarding schools, B, C and D in day schools. Study C lasted four weeks; the others lasted twelve.

task.audience: a head teacher deciding on a programme
task.prompt: Write a short briefing for Dr Mensah (90–145 words). Explain where the studies agree, where they differ and why, and what you would conclude.

points.idea: Four of the five studies found students slept longer.
The two largest studies are consistent: about 15 to 18 minutes more.
Study C found no gain, but it was much shorter (four weeks).
Study E showed the largest effect, but it was small and in a boarding school.
The likely benefit is modest but real; be cautious.

items.model: Dr Mensah, the studies mostly agree: in four of the five, students slept longer. The two largest studies, B and D, are in close agreement, with about 15 to 18 extra minutes a night. The differences are easy to explain. Study C found no gain, but it ran for only four weeks, while the others lasted twelve. Study E reported the biggest effect, 31 minutes, yet it was small and took place in a boarding school, where pupils' evenings are more controlled, so I would not rely on it. My conclusion is cautious: the programme probably gives a modest but real benefit of around a quarter of an hour, which may justify a trial, but not great expectations.
useful: The differences are easy to explain.
tips: To combine several studies, first say where they agree, then explain each exception with a reason (length, size, setting) from the notes.
Give more weight to larger studies and say so. A small outlier should be reported but not allowed to set the headline.
items.explain: The briefing needs the shared direction, the consistent 15 to 18 minutes in the larger studies, a reason for each outlier and a cautious verdict. Study A fits the general pattern and adds nothing to the decision.

items.title: Whose name is on the slide?
items.scenario: Two colleagues, Lukas and Mei, are arguing in front of you about credit for a project presentation. You are the team coordinator. Speak to both of them in a way that lowers the tension and moves them to a solution.

lines.t: I spent three weeks on the analysis, and the final slide just says "the team". Nobody even knows I did it.
You were not in the room. I stood there while the director asked questions, and I answered all of them.
Because you never invited me to come!
You were on leave. It is not my fault you were away.
That was one week, and I was still checking email.
I did the hard part, Lukas. I had to defend your numbers.

task.audience: two colleagues in a tense argument
task.prompt: Speak to Lukas and Mei (85–130 words). Acknowledge what each did, reframe the problem, and propose a concrete fix.

points.idea: Acknowledge Lukas's three weeks of analysis.
Acknowledge Mei presenting and answering the director's questions.
Reframe: not who deserves credit, but making both contributions visible.
Name both on the slide and have Lukas join the next presentation.

leave_out.idea: The argument over who was on leave.

items.model: I can hear that you both worked hard, and you each feel that part of it has gone unseen. Lukas, three weeks of careful analysis is the foundation of this project, and it should not disappear behind the word "team". Mei, you stood in front of the director and answered every question, and that was not easy either. I would like us to stop asking who deserves more credit, and ask how we make both contributions visible. So I suggest that we put both your names on the slide, and that Lukas joins the next presentation, so the director hears from both of you. Does that feel fair?
useful: I can hear that you both …
part of it has gone unseen
I would like us to stop asking … and ask …
tips: To reduce tension, validate the feeling behind each complaint ("unseen", "not easy") before you offer a fix. A complaint that is heard loses much of its heat.
Reframe a zero-sum question ("who deserves more?") as a shared problem ("how do we show both?"). Then offer a concrete step each person can see.
items.explain: The facilitator names what each did, reframes the dispute and gives a concrete fix for the slide and the next presentation. Reopening the leave argument would restart the quarrel.

items.title: A blood pressure trial in plain English
items.scenario: You write for a community health newsletter. A reader has asked about the abstract below. Rewrite it for the general public without losing accuracy or overselling the result.

text: In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 1,240 adults aged 40 to 74 with stage 1 hypertension received either a fixed low-dose combination of two antihypertensive agents or a placebo for twelve weeks. The primary outcome was the change in mean systolic blood pressure from baseline.

At twelve weeks, mean systolic pressure fell by 9.4 mmHg more in the treatment group than in the placebo group (95% confidence interval 7.8 to 11.0). Dizziness was reported by 4.1% of participants receiving the combination and 1.8% of those receiving placebo; no serious adverse events were attributed to treatment.

The authors caution that the follow-up period was short, that adults aged 75 and over and people with chronic kidney disease were excluded, and that the findings should not be extended to those groups. Longer trials are needed to establish whether the reduction is maintained and whether it lowers the risk of heart attack and stroke.

task.audience: general readers of a community health newsletter
task.prompt: Write a short article paragraph (100–155 words). Use everyday words, keep the numbers that matter and state the limits honestly.

points.idea: A low-dose pill combining two medicines was tested in adults with mildly raised blood pressure.
Blood pressure fell by about 9 points more than with a dummy pill.
Dizziness was a little more common (about 4 in 100, against 2 in 100).
Only 12 weeks; people over 75 and with kidney disease were not included.
It is not yet known whether it prevents heart attacks or strokes, so talk to a doctor.

leave_out.idea: The confidence interval and technical units.

items.model: A new study has tested a single low-dose pill that combines two blood pressure medicines. More than 1,200 adults with mildly raised blood pressure took either the pill or a dummy pill for twelve weeks. Those taking the real pill saw their top blood pressure reading fall by about 9 points more than the others. Dizziness was a little more common with the pill, affecting about 4 people in 100 compared with 2 in 100, and no serious side effects were linked to it. However, the study lasted only 12 weeks and did not include people over 75 or with kidney disease. It is also still unknown whether the pill reduces heart attacks and strokes, so please speak to your doctor before changing any treatment.
useful: please speak to your doctor before …
tips: Convert statistics into frequencies ("4 in 100") rather than percentages with decimals. Most general readers grasp them faster.
Accuracy for lay readers means including the authors' limits (short time, excluded groups, missing outcomes). Dropping them oversells the result.
items.explain: The paragraph must say what was tested, the size of the effect against a dummy pill, the side effect in frequencies, the limits of the study and what is still unknown. The confidence interval is for specialists and would not help this readership.

items.title: Must students attend lectures?
items.scenario: You write for a faculty newsletter. You attended a panel debate on compulsory attendance at lectures. Summarise the debate in a few sentences so that no speaker is misrepresented.

lines.t: I support compulsory attendance. When students sit in a room together, we notice who is struggling within the first weeks and can step in. When I was a student, my own lecturers did exactly that for me.
I understand that, but many of us work part-time or care for relatives. A fixed attendance rule punishes the students with the least flexibility, and absence is not the same as disengagement.

I think both of you are right about different things. Large lectures are the weakest place to demand presence. In seminars, where discussion is the point, attendance really matters, and I would require it only there.
Then how would we notice a student who simply disappears?
Through other signals: handed-in work, online activity, a short check-in with a tutor.
I could accept that, as long as recorded lectures stay available. On that at least, I think we all agree.
Yes, recordings should stay. I would still say that they are no substitute for being there.

task.audience: faculty newsletter readers
task.prompt: Write a neutral summary of the debate (90–140 words). Give each position fairly, note any agreement, and do not take a side.

points.idea: Professor Hale favours compulsory attendance because teachers can spot struggling students early.
Ms Ito opposes it because many students work or care for relatives and need flexibility.
Dr Reyes would require attendance only in seminars and use other signals for lectures.
All three agreed that recorded lectures should remain available.

leave_out.idea: Professor Hale's personal memory of his own student days.

items.model: The panel discussed whether lecture attendance should be compulsory and did not reach a single conclusion. Professor Hale argued in favour, saying that regular presence helps staff to notice students who are struggling and to step in early. Ms Ito disagreed, pointing out that many students work or look after relatives, so a fixed rule penalises those with the least flexibility, and absence does not necessarily mean disengagement. Dr Reyes took a middle position: attendance should be required only in seminars, with other signals such as submitted work used elsewhere. All three agreed on one point, that recorded lectures should remain available, although Professor Hale stressed that recordings cannot replace being in the room.
useful: The panel discussed whether … and did not reach …
All three agreed on one point, that …
tips: In a fair summary each speaker gets the same kind of space: position, then main reason, in similar wording. Counting sentences is a good check.
Report agreement as well as conflict, and keep each speaker's own qualifications ("only in seminars"). Hiding a qualification distorts the position.
items.explain: A balanced summary has each of the three positions with its reason, plus the one point of agreement. Hale's memory of his own studies is colour and not part of the argument.

items.title: A water notice on local radio
items.scenario: You work for the local radio station. The water company's scientist gives you this briefing. You must read a short public message on air that is clear, honest about what is not known, and does not cause panic.

text: Here is where we stand. Overnight a pump failure at the Eastfield treatment works let some water bypass the final disinfection stage for about six hours. Of the fourteen samples we have tested from the Eastfield and Millbrook districts, two show traces of E. coli. Turbidity readings were also elevated, but those numbers mean little to the public.

What does this mean? For most healthy adults the risk of becoming ill is low, and I want to say that plainly. But the risk is higher for babies, for older people, for pregnant women, and for anyone with a weakened immune system, so we are treating this seriously.

Our advice is simple. Until further notice, residents in Eastfield and Millbrook should boil tap water for one full minute and let it cool before drinking it, using it for baby feeds, brushing teeth or making ice. Water for washing and flushing toilets is fine as it is.

What we do not yet know is why the pump failed, or whether the two positive samples show a wider problem. The pump has been repaired, but we will not lift the notice until two rounds of tests, twenty-four hours apart, are clear. We expect another update on Wednesday at noon.

task.audience: radio listeners in two districts
task.prompt: Read a message for the radio (95–145 words). Give the advice, say who is most at risk, be honest about the risk and the unknowns, and say when the next update will come.

points.idea: Boil tap water for one minute before drinking, in Eastfield and Millbrook.
The risk is low for most healthy adults but higher for babies, older people and pregnant women.
The cause is not yet known and the notice stays until tests are clear.
The next update is on Wednesday at noon.

leave_out.idea: Technical details (turbidity, number of samples, pump stage).

items.model: Here is an important message for people living in Eastfield and Millbrook. Until further notice, please boil your tap water for a full minute, then let it cool before you drink it, give it to a baby or use it to brush your teeth. Water for washing and for the toilet is fine as it is. For most healthy adults the risk of illness is low. However, babies, older people and pregnant women are more vulnerable, so please follow this advice carefully. We do not yet know exactly why the problem happened, and the notice will stay in place until two rounds of tests are clear. The next update will be on Wednesday at noon. Please check on elderly neighbours.
useful: Here is an important message for …
For most people the risk is low. However, …
tips: Risk communication needs three honest layers: what to do now, how serious it really is, and what is still unknown. Do not hide uncertainty to sound calm.
On air, say the instruction once in a very clear sentence and leave out numbers the audience cannot use (sample counts, lab readings).
items.explain: Listeners need the boiling instruction and the area, who is most vulnerable, a calm statement of the low general risk, the open questions and the time of the next update. Laboratory detail adds worry without adding action.

items.title: Phones at school: a way forward
items.scenario: You chair a school council with a teacher, a parent and a student. The meeting on a phone policy has reached a deadlock. Speak to the group to turn the disagreement into something they can agree on.

lines.t: The evidence from my classroom is clear. When phones are in pockets, half the class is not listening. They should be banned during the school day, full stop.
My daughter is thirteen and gets anxious if she cannot reach us. And frankly, I pay for her phone bill; I expect her to have it. What if there is an emergency?
We also use phones for translation, calculators and timetables. And honestly, teachers look at their phones too. A total ban feels like we are not trusted.
Nobody is saying that. I am saying lessons have to be protected.
And I am saying children must be reachable. Those two things cannot both be true.
Maybe they can. I do not need my phone in a maths lesson. I just want it at lunch.

task.audience: a school council with different interests
task.prompt: Speak to the council (90–140 words). Reframe the disagreement around a shared aim, propose a workable policy and suggest how to check it.

points.idea: The shared aim is that students can learn and also feel safe and in contact.
The question is not ban or no ban, but when and how phones are used.
Phones away during lessons, allowed at breaks.
Emergencies go through the school office, so parents can always reach students.
Try it for a term and review.

leave_out.idea: The phone bill and the remark about teachers' phones.

items.model: Thank you all. I think there is more agreement here than it seems. Everyone wants students to learn without distraction, and everyone wants them to be safe and reachable. So perhaps the question is not whether to ban phones, but when and how they are used. May I suggest this? Phones stay away during lessons, and students can use them at break and lunch. If a parent needs to reach a child urgently, they call the school office, and the office passes the message on straight away. We run this for one term, and then the council reviews it together with the students' own feedback. Could each of you accept that as a starting point?
useful: There is more agreement here than it seems.
The question is not whether …, but when and how …
Could each of you accept that as a starting point?
tips: In a deadlock, look for the sentence everybody can sign ("students should learn and be safe") and rebuild the disagreement as a design question about when and how.
Make each side's real need part of the solution (lessons protected, parents able to reach), so no one has to lose in order for the others to win.
items.explain: The chair names the shared aim, changes the question to when and how, gives a rule with an emergency route and sets a review. The phone bill and the remark about teachers' own phones are side issues that would reopen the quarrel.

items.title: The bus network decision
items.scenario: The transport department has produced a long options report. The mayor and cabinet decide on Friday and have only minutes to read. Write a precise briefing note with the essential points.

text: Three options for the regional bus network were assessed.

Option A, patching the existing network, would cost about 4 million a year and leave ridership flat. Roughly a third of the vehicles reach the end of their working life in 2029, and the replacement cost is not included in the figure.

Option B, a core-frequency network, concentrates service on the twelve busiest routes, running buses every ten minutes. It requires 11 million of capital spending over three years. Modelling suggests an increase of 18% in passengers on core routes. To pay for it, six low-use rural routes would be replaced by an on-demand minibus service, which has been well received in the one town where it was tested but remains unproven at scale.

Option C, a full redesign including new depots and traffic-priority lanes, would cost 24 million over five years and is projected to raise ridership by 30%. It would cause disruption on main roads for about three years. It depends on a state grant covering half of the cost; applications close on 30 September, and approval is not guaranteed.

The consultation received 3,200 responses, with a majority favouring more frequent services. Officers' view is that Option B delivers most of the benefit at the lowest risk, and that it can be designed so that a move to Option C remains possible if the grant is awarded.
The decision needed on Friday is whether to proceed with Option B and, separately, whether to submit the grant application for Option C before the deadline.

task.audience: the mayor and cabinet, who have a few minutes
task.prompt: Write a briefing note (90–140 words). Recommend an option, give the main benefit, the main cost or risk, and the deadline.

points.idea: Officers recommend Option B (11 million over three years).
B is expected to raise passengers on core routes by 18%.
The cost: six rural routes become an on-demand service, which is unproven at scale.
The grant application for Option C closes on 30 September and is uncertain.

items.model: Recommendation: proceed with Option B, the core-frequency network, at a capital cost of 11 million over three years. It keeps frequent service on the twelve busiest routes and is expected to raise core-route ridership by 18%, with the least risk of the three options. The main trade-off is that six low-use rural routes would be swapped for a minibus service on demand, which worked in one town but is unproven at scale. Option C offers more, 30% growth, but depends on a state grant that is not guaranteed. The grant application closes on 30 September, so a separate decision is needed on Friday. Option B can be designed to keep Option C possible.
useful: a separate decision is needed on …
can be designed to keep … possible
tips: For top decision makers, lead with the recommendation and keep to a handful of precise points: benefit, trade-off, deadline. Everything else is on request.
Make the decision in front of them explicit, including any decision that is separate (the grant) and its date.
items.explain: The note needs the recommended option and its cost, the headline benefit, the rural-route trade-off and uncertainty, and the grant deadline. The number of consultation responses is supporting evidence that does not change the decision.
